sections.title: Human Friction
description: Within the Ubisoft Creator Program, over 14,000 partner creators felt invisible. Producing high-effort content with zero brand feedback directly eroded creator retention and community trust.

sections.title: Business Opportunity
description: Massive volumes of partner content went unexploited. Ubisoft left significant potential Earned Media Value (EMV) on the table because internal teams lacked a structured approach.
Working as the primary UX designer under the guidance of my Design Manager, my goal was to define an operational strategy that bridged this dual gap within strict enterprise constraints.

sections.title: Discovery
description: To validate creator friction, I executed a two-pronged discovery phase. First, I conducted an external public benchmark across 12 entertainment brands (including EA, Riot, and LEGO). This revealed that while macro-influencers received dedicated PR spotlighting, no competitor offered a visible, structured recognition system for micro and nano-creators.

Concurrently, I audited 20+ partner channels and analyzed 60+ Discord community reports. This research confirmed that creator dissatisfaction stemmed from an operational void: creators produced content in a complete vacuum, lacking feedback loops or clear channels for internal discovery.

sections.title: Cross-Functional Co-Design
description: Because creator invisibility was rooted in backend operational confusion, I focused ideation on internal stakeholders rather than external creators who could not resolve internal handoff mechanics.

sections.title: Strategic Frameworks
description: I structured and facilitated a 2-hour 20-minute workshop, inviting leads specifically for their daily proximity to partner creators and domain expertise.

Using an Impact/Effort matrix, we evaluated 24 concepts and converged on official channel reposting as our primary mechanism. This collaborative session also served to identify which key departments needed to be formally integrated into the eventual pipeline.

sections.title: Workflow Refinement
description: Following the workshop, I conducted deep-dive interviews with leads across flagship AAA titles. This revealed the project's true organizational complexity: 6 separate departments needed to collaborate across fragmented toolchains (combining publishing tools, task trackers, and community hubs).
Across 5 iterative cycles, I engineered the workflow to introduce mandatory Brand Safety validation gates while decoupling global asset vetting from local market publishing.

sections.title: Large-Scale Validation
description: Once the internal workflow was established, I designed a quantitative survey framework for the 2,000+ Discord creator community to verify creator interest, receptivity, and buy-in prior to live rollout.

sections.title: RACI Governance
description: To turn this multi-department workflow into clear enterprise governance, I structured the process into an operational RACI framework. I defined two distinct execution pathways: a Proactive model for planned campaign activations and a Reactive model for spontaneous community clips.

sections.title: Persuasive Storytelling
description: To secure executive buy-in, I translated these models into visual storyboards. By mapping the end-to-end human journey (from a creator's Discord submission through Brand Safety approval to local channel publishing), these visuals transformed complex technical handoffs into an engaging, accessible story.
This narrative approach secured 100% executive approval across all 3 key department leads, delivering a production-ready operational blueprint for trial rollout.

sections.title: Impact and Reflections
description: This project reinforced my core conviction that a great solution is not merely usable on paper, but actively adopted and embraced by its operational users.

Navigating strict 30-minute availability limits with internal staff taught me to design highly efficient interview protocols. When third-party dependencies created project downtime, I maintained momentum by executing baseline comparative usability evaluations for an internal creator administration platform.

Ultimately, it proved that visual storytelling is one of the most effective ways to bridge technical systems and business decision-makers, turning complex operational proposals into compelling, buy-in-ready initiatives.

main.title: VMT
main.description: optimizing cognitive affordance in industrial CAD training

sections.title: Context
description: When Airbus Helicopters built the Virtual Maintenance Trainer, a 3D simulation platform designed to train aeronautical technicians on complex maintenance procedures, they created a tool with high-fidelity technical modeling that ultimately struggled to gain traction in actual classrooms.

sections.title: Diagnostic Challenge
description: The core problem was a total breakdown in adoption. Instructors were actively bypassing the digital simulator during live lessons, falling back on physical mockups or paper manuals. Because physical aviation mockups are scarce and expensive to maintain, abandoning the digital platform created severe training bottlenecks around technician certification timelines.

sections.title: Scope
description: Operating as an embedded UX Consultant through the IMS Laboratory, my goal was to uncover the cognitive and ergonomic root causes behind this resistance and realign the interface with actual classroom workflows.

sections.title: Discovery
description: To immerse myself in the environment and understand the software's baseline operation, I conducted an initial heuristic walkthrough to identify purely technical friction points, such as basic navigational dead ends. Alongside reviewing three aeronautical doctoral theses on simulation learning, this initial audit allowed me to build a highly targeted, semi-directive interview grid tailored to the Airbus training context.

sections.title: Qualitative Research
description: During this early phase, a key insight emerged: B2 Avionics instructors adapted to the software with ease, whereas B1.3 Mechanical instructors rejected it entirely because the digital environment offered zero tactile feedback for physical engine parts. Armed with my interview grid, I headed to Aérocampus Aquitaine to conduct seven in-depth interviews with instructors and trainees, processing the audio rapidly via WhisperAI.

sections.title: Field Discoveries
description: When observing live classes, I noted that instructors naturally gravitated toward physical mockups rather than opening the 3D software. I pivoted my methodology toward informal contextual inquiries between sessions, which revealed that the navigational overhead of setting up the software severely disrupted their instructional pacing.

sections.title: Quantitative Triangulation
description: To back up these qualitative insights with hard data, I deployed a primary survey to active instructors to measure system usability and task friction. I then triangulated my 11 primary survey responses with a historical internal Airbus study of 18 VMT users, creating a consolidated and highly relevant dataset of 29 participants.
The data proved the issue was systemic: 70% of instructors used the software less than once a month, and 55% cited 3D camera movement and interface clarity as major blockers.

sections.title: Heuristic Synthesis
description: With my raw data collected, I needed a way to objectively classify my findings. I adopted the 10-Point Ergonomic Heuristic Framework by Colombo and Pasch to synthesize the interview and survey data, evaluating vectors like Ergonomic Transparency and Cognitive Load.

sections.title: Usability Diagnosis
description: This structural analysis allowed me to map a total of 28 distinct usability issues across the platform. From this comprehensive diagnosis, I engineered 25 concrete ergonomic recommendations, ranging from architectural menu reorganizations to permissive interaction models. To keep this case study focused, I have isolated the top three most severe cognitive friction points:

• Unstandardized camera navigation disoriented users during engine inspections.
• Nested menus constantly forced instructors to look away from the task while lecturing.
• Selecting small 3D engine components required pinpoint mouse accuracy with zero visual hover affordance.

sections.title: Interaction Specification
description: Because my mandate focused on interaction architecture rather than high-fidelity visual assets, I developed ergonomic interaction specifications to solve these exact issues.
I proposed a dual-mode camera system combining standard WASD movement for navigating rooms with automatic orbit controls centered on selected components.
To reduce menu dependency, I designed a cursor-anchored radial menu leveraging Fitts's Law to give instant access to key actions.
Finally, I specified permissive click tolerances, dynamic component outlining, and structured error messages to eliminate guesswork.

sections.title: Impact and Reflections
description: The final deliverables included a 63-page comprehensive UX analysis report detailing all 28 usability blockers and their corresponding 25 technical specifications. To ensure actionable stakeholder buy-in, I distilled this exhaustive report into an executive slide presentation that pitched the six most impactful strategic ideas.

This specification package (bridging the comprehensive research report and the focused executive pitch) received unanimous sign-off from engineering leads at Airbus Helicopters and Telespazio for integration into production.

Looking back, pivoting away from formal observations to capture contextual setups proved that even highly detailed technical simulations fail if the underlying interaction design ignores human cognitive limits.

main.title: Emco
main.description: decoupling emotional state from cognitive workload

sections.title: Context
sections.description: Corporate ergonomists evaluate workplace quality of life and prevent psychosocial risks, but traditional methods rely heavily on retrospective, subjective questionnaires. The EmCo project aimed to create an objective diagnostic system translating non-invasive biometric telemetry into actionable Quality of Work Life (QVT) indicators.

sections.title: Scientific Challenge
description: Emotion and cognition activate similar physiological responses but operate on fundamentally different temporal scales: emotion manifests as sudden, brief physiological spikes, whereas cognition represents sustained resource mobilization. The core UX challenge was visually decoupling these biological realities without overwhelming the user with raw data.
As the UX Lead across a six-person cross-disciplinary team, I owned the information architecture and technical UI decisions, tasked with delivering a complete 20-screen mobile design system.

sections.title: Data Translation
sections.description: Raw data is useless without interpretation. To prevent cognitive overload, I translated complex biometric streams (HRV, EDA) into actionable, human-readable status labels like 'Focus Productif' and 'Surcharge Critique'.

sections.title: Privacy
sections.description: To handle privacy seamlessly during live monitoring, I implemented iOS-style FaceID; this allowed ergonomists to securely and repeatedly lift patient anonymity for clinical checks without the long-term interaction friction of passwords.

sections.title: Rapid Execution
sections.description: Operating within a strict 5-day conceptual sprint, I aggressively timeboxed the high-fidelity UI execution to just 48 hours. To maximize efficiency, I utilized AI Studio to audit wireframe layouts before executing Day 3 usability testing with 5 cognitive engineering professors and PhD researchers acting as proxy users.

sections.title: Usability Evaluation
sections.description: AttrakDiff testing revealed high engagement (+1.5 Stimulation) but highlighted a critical usability flaw (-0.5 Pragmatic Quality), as continuous 3D emotional heatmaps proved too dense to interpret during extended monitoring.

sections.title: Empirical Iteration
description: To eliminate this cognitive friction, I executed three targeted architectural changes to aggressively filter visual noise:

• I abandoned the dense heatmaps in favor of a flattened grid based on Russell's model. By plotting discrete subject markers, the eye is instantly guided to critical outliers rather than scanning a chaotic 3D map.
• I paired this grid with a temporal scrubbing slider, empowering users to track short emotional peaks over time and isolate them from baseline cognitive fatigue.
• I added explicit threshold baselines across all cognitive and biometric charts to remove interpretive guesswork, and consolidated ambient header actions into a labeled hamburger menu to keep the screen focused purely on diagnostic tasks.

sections.title: Impact and Reflections
description: Delivering a functional MedTech design system under extreme time limits required aggressive scoping of core user flows. Using AI tools to critique wireframes accelerated iteration loops, while negative pragmatic feedback highlighted the danger of over-designing real-time charts.

Although the sprint's timeline precluded a second round of testing, the final architectural pivot was designed specifically to let users instantly differentiate acute stress events from baseline recovery. The project culminated in strong validation from the reviewing panel.

If transitioned into a commercial product, the immediate strategic next step would be deploying the iterated prototype in the field: conducting rigorous usability testing with practicing corporate ergonomists to validate the UI changes and refine the QVT indicators for enterprise adoption.

main.shortDescription: decoupling emotional state from cognitive workload

sections.title: Strategic Pivot
description: Tasked initially with a superficial UI refresh, I deployed quantitative research across 300+ respondents to validate the founders' core hypothesis: replacing commodified swipe mechanics with synchronous video connections. The data confirmed the viability of this strategy, revealing a 77.5% rejection rate of traditional swipe interfaces among users experiencing severe market exhaustion.

sections.title: Time-Boxed Mechanics
description: To execute this vision, I engineered a real-time interaction hub restricted to a dedicated 18h-22h window to artificially drive concurrent user density and dismantle choice fatigue. To offset the restricted active window, I designed a frictionless monetization flow integrating premium tier subscriptions and single-use micro-transactions for immediate encounter refills.

sections.title: High-Stakes Interaction Design
description: The core product loop centers on a time-boxed 5-minute live audio-visual call, requiring a hyper-focused UI to manage cognitive load.

sections.title: Accessibility
description: I proposed the structural integration of real-time automated text transcription overlays to ensure hearing inclusivity, and engineered an immediate mutual 'Spark' decision gate to filter access to direct messaging.

Knowing 56% of female users face harassment, I designed a low-friction, persistent safety reporting flow that allows users to instantly block and report abusers without breaking the overarching navigation architecture.

sections.title: Tokenized Architecture
description: To support the complex technical requirements of live video and asynchronous messaging, I architected a tokenized Figma design system utilizing 60+ variables to seamlessly manage the brand’s dark-mode primary theme and neon interactive accents. This systematized approach eliminated design debt, ensuring rapid developer handoff across 7 fully prototyped interactive flows and 100+ high-fidelity states.

sections.title: Brand Execution
description: The final deliverable included bespoke iconography, Apple HIG-compliant PACE microcopy, and a comprehensive investor pitch deck that successfully positioned the human-centered UX strategy as a viable market disruptor.

sections.title: Sprint Context
description: Following the Double Diamond framework, this intensive multi-product sprint simulated fast-paced agency conditions across three separate product domains. The core objective was to rapidly adapt to unfamiliar industries, conduct targeted contextual research, build modular Figma design systems, and execute empirical field testing under real-world constraints.

sections.title: Phase 1: Conceptual Architecture (Ridar, Urban Mobility Security)
Field Observations
description: Urban bicycle theft results in 400,000 stolen bikes annually in France. To identify behavioral root causes, we conducted contextual observations and interviews in high-traffic transit hubs across Bordeaux, including Sainte-Catherine Street and Bergonié.

sections.title: Research Insights
description: While mapping three distinct personas (the delivery driver, the rushed parent, and the determined ecologist), our research pinpointed micro-stops as the most critical point of vulnerability. The primary friction point was time: the 23.2-second average required to secure a physical U-lock leads cyclists making brief stops to bypass security entirely to maintain their delivery schedules.

sections.title: Ideation
description: To avoid generic security clichés, our team ran a 15-minute ideation purge to eliminate obvious concepts, leaving a dozen viable ideas. We evaluated these on a matrix structured along two axes: Standalone Hardware vs. Bike-Integrated, and Passive Security vs. Smart Monitoring.

sections.title: Prioritization
description: Scoring the surviving concepts on effectiveness, feasibility, and originality birthed Ridar: a phygital security device integrated directly into the seat post. It auto-arms in the background as the cyclist walks away, completely eliminating the 23.2-second physical lock friction.

sections.title: Visual Storyboarding
description: As Co-Researcher, I illustrated the core user workflow through a storyboard centered on Rayan, a delivery driver persona. The storyboard demonstrates how Ridar passively protects his bike without requiring manual app interaction during quick pick-ups. The system issues instant smartphone alerts and triggers a localized physical alarm upon detecting unauthorized motion, protecting his primary source of income without compromising his delivery speed.

sections.title: Phase 2: Systems Design (DeskFriend, Remote Workspace Ergonomics)
Specification Audit Rescoping
description: Transitioning to workspace ergonomics, our team inherited an external student spec sheet for a smart desk controller. The initial proposal suffered from severe feature bloat, presenting 11 fragmented themes (some packing up to three sub-features each).
Rather than executing flawed requirements, we held a structured brainstorming session to rationally rescope the project, consolidating the scattered ideas into 4 core UX pillars.

sections.title: Rapid Architecture
description: To align the team without losing momentum, we drove rapid consensus through low-fidelity whiteboard wireframing, mapping the 4 pillars into a streamlined control interface with 6 modular UI cards.

sections.title: Prototyping
description: Stepping in as Visual Design Lead, I engineered the high-fidelity Figma prototype from scratch using Auto Layout rules, tokenized color palettes, and reusable component libraries.

The flagship UX feature was a physical Focus Mode: users dock their smartphone onto the desk controller, transforming the phone into a tactile workspace remote while automatically filtering out non-essential digital notifications.

sections.title: Phase 3: Field Testing (Smart Cart, Autonomous Retail Usability)
Testing Protocol
description: In the final phase, we evaluated an unbuilt 100L autonomous supermarket cart concept designed by a third team. I co-designed a guerrilla field usability test at a Leclerc supermarket in Pessac with 9 real shoppers.

To evaluate spatial navigation efficiently, we engineered a hybrid testing protocol pairing an interactive Figma mobile app with a physical cardboard store map and a cart token, allowing us to evaluate shopper mental models without requiring full-store physical walks.

sections.title: Findings
description: Testing yielded a 100% completion rate for cart pairing but exposed foundational flaws in the product's premise. Five out of nine shoppers bypassed the digital checkout flow. Our protocol revealed a physical reflex trade-off: having a physical cart token in hand caused users' ingrained habit of pushing a cart to a cashier to override the digital UI prompt.

More critically, participants overwhelmingly stated a preference for paper grocery lists over the digital application, noting that the app caused them to 'lose the initiative to think'. Shoppers saw zero personal utility in the software, proving the digital feature set was a complex solution to an unvalidated problem.

sections.title: Impact and Reflections
description: This design relay demonstrated that effective UX leadership requires ruthless prioritization and the courage to challenge flawed assumptions.
Navigating specification ambiguity in Phase 2 proved that structured low-fidelity wireframing prevents engineering waste and accelerates scalable Figma design systems.

Ultimately, Phase 3 reinforced that high-fidelity UI cannot salvage a product that fails to address a genuine human need: true product strategy prioritizes observing real human behavior over forcing unnecessary digital adoption.

projects.title: Card sorting
projects.shortDescription: aligning enterprise tooling with student mental models

sections.title: Academic Context
description: Restructuring a 33-service university portal into an intuitive 12-category taxonomy through in-person Open Card Sorting, 33x33 Similarity Matrix quantification, and semantic jargon decoupling.

sections.title: Operational Bottleneck
description: The Bordeaux INP digital workspace housed 33 essential administrative, academic, and technical tools within a flat, unstructured grid. Built around institutional silos rather than user cognition, the interface lacked thematic grouping, forcing exhaustive visual scanning.

sections.title: Strategic Approach
description: To restructure this architecture, I co-led a mixed-methods Open Card Sorting study, prioritizing the student cohort as the primary daily users to establish a baseline behavioral taxonomy.

sections.title: Mixed-Methods Synthesis & Semantic Overhaul
description: To mitigate the risks of a localized sample size (N=9), we triangulated qualitative verbatim audits with a strict quantitative 33x33 Similarity Matrix to calculate functional co-occurrence. This data pipeline revealed a 100% correlation between the timetable (ADE) and the learning platform (Moodle), dictating the creation of a prioritized 'Essentiels' tier.

Furthermore, qualitative analysis exposed that vendor names and institutional acronyms severely disrupted navigation. I resolved this by decoupling 7 jargon bottlenecks, injecting immediate functional affordance—such as renaming the opaque 'Marsha' to 'Visioconférence - Marsha' and 'ODF' to 'Offre de Formation'.

sections.title: Scalable Architecture
description: The research culminated in a functional Figma prototype that successfully condensed the 33 fragmented tools into 12 user-validated, alphabetically sub-sorted categories (e.g., Administratif, Mobilité, Assistance).

sections.title: Role-Based Strategy
description: More importantly, the similarity matrix isolated low-frequency, ambiguous items like 'Evacataires'. Rather than forcing these into the student taxonomy, we leveraged these outliers to advocate for a dynamic, role-personalized portal architecture, ensuring that the interface adapts to the distinct requirements of students, faculty, and administrative staff.

sections.title: Challenge
description: At ENSC, engineering students are required to rapidly build interactive UI prototypes for cross-disciplinary projects, user testing, and stakeholder presentations. Without formal training in design system architecture, students relied on trial-and-error execution.
This resulted in fragile component hierarchies, broken layouts, and inconsistent interfaces that compromised both the integrity of live user testing and eventual developer handoffs.

sections.title: Architecting the Solution
description: To replace guesswork with standardized product logic, I independently architected a 90+ slide curriculum natively within Figma, structured across 6 modular learning tracks.
To prevent cognitive overload, I avoided static screenshots and instead designed explicit vector diagrams to visually map out abstract mechanics like Auto Layout grids,frame nesting, and variables.

To bridge theory and practice, I am developing a suite of hands-on, atomic tutorials mirroring the students' actual academic deliverables. These exercises guide students progressively through constructing scalable Auto Layout buttons, building multi-state component sets, and correctly mapping design tokens (variables) to control UI logic.

sections.title: Proactive Handoff
sections.description: Following iterative peer validation to resolve technical edge cases, I proactively delivered this production-ready framework to the ENSC faculty. As a self-initiated contribution, my objective was to provide non-expert professors with a reliable teaching asset.

sections.title: Knowledge Sharing
sections.description: By open-sourcing this curriculum to the institution, the goal is to empower future engineering cohorts to autonomously build robust, testable prototypes that align with professional software standards.

sections.title: Challenge
description: During an internship at ENSC, I was challenged to introduce 15 high school students from the 'Cordées de la réussite' equal-opportunity program to UX design and cognitive engineering.
Professional tools like Figma often cause cognitive overload for beginners. My goal was to strip away the complexity and design a 4-hour workshop that was accessible, engaging, and highly practical

sections.title: Pedagogical Interaction
description: To ensure the students could work autonomously, I designed a multi-tiered learning experience. I first built a dynamic, 30-minute interactive presentation natively inside Figma to demonstrate frames, layers, and typography in real-time.

I then coded a custom HTML/CSS portal hosting step-by-step video tutorials. Before the workshop, I tested this portal with a Figma novice to measure time-on-task and identify potential usability bottlenecks, adjusting the pacing to fit our tight 4-hour window.

sections.title: The Agency Simulation
description: The workshop culminated in a 2.5-hour hands-on sprint where students worked in three groups to design 'Orchestra,' a desktop music streaming application. Acting as the client, I provided strict brand guidelines and specific feature requirements, including a dedicated 'Handi-sons' section to introduce the students to the core concepts of accessibility and inclusive design.

sections.title: Impact & Facilitation
description: Despite the challenges of maintaining engagement over a long session, every team successfully delivered a multi-page wireframe with functional navigation filters.

I actively coached the groups through interface friction, teaching them how to resolve layer hierarchy and alignment issues. The sprint concluded with the students pitching their UX decisions, proving that with the right structural support, novices can quickly grasp and apply professional design thinking.

playgrounds.title: kfé
playgrounds.shortDescription: redesign of a coffee shop's mobile app

sections.title: Navigating Ambiguity
description: Operating under severe time constraints with highly ambiguous stakeholder directives, I led the agile discovery phase to extract and define core product mechanics.

Through targeted requirement gathering, I isolated rigid business constraints that dictated the initial system architecture: strict adherence to corporate branding, fixed three-tier sizing, and limited modification parameters (milk and sugar). This foundational logic informed the data structure required to calculate dynamic cart totals and combined product pricing before any interface was drafted.

sections.title: Interaction Architecture
description: To optimize the legacy interface, I conducted a heuristic optimization sprint focused on minimizing user cognitive load and friction. I abandoned traditional multi-screen modification flows in favor of engineering complex, multi-state in-line expansion cards directly on the main menu. Utilizing tactile segmented controls and dot sliders, users can fully customize their beverage without ever losing their primary browsing context.

This structural shift was paired with a visual overhaul rooted in culinary psychology: replacing rigid corporate greens with warm oranges and coffee-browns to maximize food affordance and stimulate user engagement.

sections.title: Adaptive Checkout
description: The checkout architecture was engineered to dynamically adapt to fulfillment intent, preventing user errors. 'Delivery' mode strictly locks payment calls-to-action until address validation is complete, while 'Pickup' mode defaults to geolocation-based store routing and surfaces immediate hardware payment options (Apple Pay).

sections.title: Edge Case Management
description: To systematically increase Average Order Value (AOV), the flow integrates a receipt-style cart layout with an inline cross-selling module 'Want a snack with that?'.
Post-purchase anxiety is mitigated through continuous system visibility, satisfying core stakeholder requirements via a multi-stage visual preparation timeline and a persistent status bar.

sections.title: Scalable Component System
description: To support these dynamic interactions, I architected a highly scalable UI kit. Rather than relying on dozens of static screens, I built a modular Figma system utilizing advanced variants and boolean properties, allowing a minimal set of base components to effortlessly handle the exponential combinations of sizes, modifiers, and cart states.

playgrounds.title: mates
playgrounds.shortDescription: comprehensive brand ecosystem and print assets

sections.title: Challenge
description: The founders of Mates, a peer-to-peer student note-sharing platform, required a brand identity that communicated community trust and pack strength without feeling overly academic.
They provided strict visual constraints:

• integrate the letter M
• use a wolf or ant motif
• employ the Inter typeface
• utilize a vibrant blue/orange palette

sections.title: Strategic Execution
description: To satisfy the structural requirements, I engineered a highly scalable logo that subtly embeds the letter 'M' into the ears of a howling wolf, symbolizing mutual support. To ensure maximum visual balance across micro-icons and campus banners, I constructed the mark using precise mathematical grid lines, geometric tangents, and circular arcs.

Recognizing that the requested blue/orange palette could cause accessibility friction on digital interfaces, I proactively presented side-by-side Figma explorations. This structured iteration successfully pivoted the stakeholders to a sleeker, high-contrast palette of Byzantine Blue (#194DDF) and Eerie Black (#212121).

sections.title: Brand System
description: Beyond the core logo, I developed a complete suite of digital and physical assets, including responsive dark-mode badges, custom illustrations, and customized headers for multiple social platforms. For physical campus marketing, I designed A5 flyer templates optimized for quick scanning, ensuring the layouts accommodated necessary visual hierarchy and spacing for future legal print compliance.

sections.title: Figma Handoff
description: The project culminated in a complete transfer of all deliverables via a systematically organized Figma library, equipping the founders with a production-ready brand system to deploy autonomously.

playgrounds.title: krystal
playgrounds.shortDescription: elements visual identity for sports events

sections.title: Context
description: Krystal is the premier annual sports tournament for the Bordeaux INP network, bringing together over 500 students and supporters across eight engineering schools. I was re-engaged for the 2026 edition to create a complete garment branding system around an 'Elemental Forces' theme within a strict two-week deadline.
The critical constraint: a strict two-week delivery deadline for all production-ready assets, with garment manufacturing limited to single-color screen printing on diverse fabric colors.

sections.title: Modular Architecture
description: To meet the aggressive timeline without sacrificing visual quality, I abandoned traditional, highly custom illustration in favor of a modular design framework. I engineered a '50/50 split-diamond' architecture.

• The lower half of the diamond was standardized across all designs, establishing a non-negotiable visual anchor that unified the eight schools.
• The upper half was customized for each assigned element.
This abstraction drastically reduced visual noise, ensuring immediate brand recognition on small chest badges while treating graphic design exactly like a scalable UI component library.

sections.title: Agile Prototyping
description: Operating within a 14-day window left zero room for vector-level revisions. I shifted 100% of the ideation phase to high-fidelity paper prototyping, generating high volumes of sketches to secure stakeholder alignment before opening design software.

This paper-first strategy kept the workflow highly efficient and completely natural. Concrete themes like Fire and Water were approved instantly from fifteen rough sketches, while complex metaphors like Time and Spirit were resolved offline by rapidly generating twenty-four concepts each. Securing this stakeholder alignment on paper eliminated digital revisions and saved days of production time.

sections.title: Technical Craft
description: Garment usability requires strict adherence to physical production constraints. Because each of the eight schools wore distinct T-shirt colors, I engineered every logo as a high-contrast, scalable SVG utilizing strategic line weight and negative space to imply 3D volume.

sections.title: Handoff
description: Every vector asset was delivered in production-ready light and dark colorways. This single-pass digital execution allowed garment vendors to print directly onto colored fabrics flawlessly, with absolutely zero post-handoff feedback required.

sections.title: Retrospective
description: Krystal 2026 proved that creativity flourishes under extreme constraints when governed by systems-level thinking. By rebuilding the brand into a modular visual architecture and enforcing strict offline alignment, I delivered a cleaner, more cohesive identity system in two weeks than traditional methods allow in two months.
